Cycles through the source, such as f[1,0]=6 and f[2,0]=20, inflate the objective above the true flow. Flow returning to node 0 should not count, so the objective is wrong. The correct objective is F (net flow), or inflow into the sink.

The reported 123 is therefore not a valid max flow. The net flow is 82, which is just the sum of the capacities out of node 0 excluding the returned flow. With the true capacities, the answer would likely differ from 82 as well. The real matrix probably has many zero entries, so the defaults are suspect.

The real capacities from nodes 1-7 into 8 are likely sizable, and the max flow could well be 123 if they are large enough. The source cut is a hard upper bound of 123, so the true answer is at most 123. With random capacities up to about 20 on a dense graph, reaching the source cut is plausible, though not certain.

The model's arc into 8 from node 1 carries 11 and from node 2 carries 0, so it needs only moderate capacities. The true values are uncertain, which gives a reasonable chance the answer is 123 but a real risk it is lower.

The model also adds arcs that flow back into the source and arcs that flow out of the sink. These are harmless on their own, but they show the arcs were fabricated.

The model additionally sets (3,8)=20 from the phrase "up to 20 from Data Center 3". The text does not clearly say that capacity is exactly 20. The same goes for (2,4)=19, which the text calls only the highest capacity out of node 2.

Since the matrix is unknown, the model's result of 123 cannot be trusted. Its source arcs sum to 6+20+15+9+20+17+16+20 = 123, so the answer is just the total capacity out of the source. That is an upper bound, and the real max flow is likely lower given the zeros in the real network.
